opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the biggest thing was that we didn't treat it as "research builds a model, then product figures out what to do with it." From day one, the people training the model and the people designing the interface were in the same room, literally debating the same questions. Like, what does it mean for the model to decide on its own when to open a canvas? How should it make targeted edits versus rewriting the whole document? Those are both model behavior questions and product questions at the same time, and you can't really separate them.

So when product had an idea, say inline comments or suggested edits, research could immediately ask, okay, what data do we need, how do we evaluate whether the model is actually good at this? And when research found the model was doing something weird, like over-triggering canvas for simple questions, the product folks could tell us whether that actually hurt the user experience or whether it was fine. That tight feedback loop let us iterate really fast.

The other piece is that it forced us to be very concrete about evals. Instead of vague goals like "make the model better at writing," we had to define specific behaviors tied to real user interactions, and a lot of that came from synthetic data generation. We used things like distilling from stronger models to teach new behaviors quickly, without needing tons of human data collection. That only works if you know exactly what product experience you're aiming for.

And honestly, I think that's going to be how a lot of AI products get built going forward. The model *is* the product in many ways, so the line between research and product design gets really blurry. Canvas was a good example of leaning into that rather than fighting it.

r001.rationale: The response describes close collaboration between research and product on model behavior and interface design, but it does not say that behavior unsuitable for model implementation was handled at the application layer with applied engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is that when research and product are separate, you end up with this handoff problem. Researchers train a model against some set of evals, they throw it over the wall, and then the product team discovers that the thing people actually want to do with it doesn't match what the model was optimized for. By the time you learn that, you're a training run behind.

With Canvas, we didn't do that. The product idea and the model behavior were being designed at the same time, by people sitting in the same room. So very early on we had questions like, when should the model open a canvas versus just answering inline? When a user highlights a paragraph and says "make this punchier," should it rewrite only that selection or touch the whole document? Those sound like product questions, but they're actually model behavior questions. You can't solve them with UI alone. The model has to understand the intent and the editing affordances. So we were writing evals for exactly those behaviors while the interface was still being prototyped, and the two informed each other constantly.

The other thing is that it let us be honest about what the model couldn't do yet. If you design the product first, you tend to promise an experience and then try to force the model into it. If you design them together, you can shape the interface around the model's real strengths and quietly route around its weaknesses, and then close those gaps with targeted post-training rather than hacks.

And frankly, it changed the culture of the team. Researchers got to watch real people use the thing, which is incredibly motivating and also humbling, because the failure modes you see in the wild are never the ones you imagined. I think that tight loop, where a user complaint on Monday can become a training signal by the end of the week, is what let Canvas feel coherent instead of feeling like a chat model with a document bolted on.

r001.rationale: The response says the interface could be shaped around the model’s strengths and route around its weaknesses, but it does not explain that unsuitable behavior was handled at the application layer in collaboration with applied engineers.

astra-6.text:
I think it helped because the model behavior and the user experience really needed to be designed together. With something like Canvas, you’re not just asking, “Can the model write or code?” You’re asking, “How does it collaborate with someone on a piece of work?” When should it make an edit directly? When should it leave a suggestion? How much of the document should it change?

Those are product questions, but they also become research questions. If you work on them separately, you can end up with a model that’s capable but doesn’t behave the way the interface leads people to expect. Bringing research and product together early creates a tighter feedback loop: you try an interaction, see where the model falls short, and use that to inform both the model and the design.

So I think the benefit is that you’re building toward a shared idea of what good collaboration feels like, rather than treating the interface as something you add after the model is finished.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helped because the research problem and the interaction design were so connected. With Canvas, you’re moving from asking a question and getting an answer to working together on something—a piece of writing or code. So the model needs to understand when to make a small edit, when to rewrite more broadly, and when to leave things alone. And the interface needs to make those choices understandable to the user.

When research and product work together from the beginning, you can iterate on both sides. A product prototype can reveal a model behavior you need to improve, and a model improvement can open up a better interaction. That feedback loop helps you build something that feels coherent, because the model and the experience are being developed around the same user need.

r001.rationale: The response describes joint iteration between research and product, but does not say that behavior unsuitable for the model was handled in the application layer with applied engineers.
